evidenceAudit.scope: Adults with known or suspected COPD presenting with an acute exacerbation to the emergency department. Verified against GOLD 2024 (Chapter 4), NICE NG115 (section 1.3) and the Saudi Thoracic Society 2025 COPD guideline.
findings: GOLD Figures 4.3 and 4.8 (ROME thresholds and NIV indications) are images in the PDF and were not text-extractable; NIV triggers are therefore stated as NICE/GOLD text describes them.
Every dose, threshold and timing was checked against the cited source section on 12 Oct 2026.
Normal values are typical adult reference ranges; laboratories differ.
unverifiedSections: Exact pH/PaCO2 thresholds to start NIV (GOLD Figure 4.8) — follow local NIV protocol
Bronchodilator and antibiotic doses — hospital formulary

pathophysiology.summary: An exacerbation (ECOPD) is increased dyspnoea and/or cough and sputum worsening over less than 14 days, often with tachypnoea and tachycardia. Airway infection (mostly viral), pollution or other insults increase airway and systemic inflammation, mucus and gas trapping. Dyspnoea is the key symptom.
keyMechanisms: Triggers: respiratory viruses (rhinovirus, influenza, parainfluenza, metapneumovirus) are the main cause; bacteria (H. influenzae, S. pneumoniae, M. catarrhalis; Pseudomonas in severe or long-standing COPD), fine particulate air pollution and excess heat also trigger events.
Increased airway inflammation and mucus with expiratory flow limitation cause dynamic hyperinflation (gas trapping), increased work of breathing and breathlessness.
Ventilation–perfusion mismatch causes hypoxaemia; respiratory muscle fatigue and hypoventilation cause hypercapnia and respiratory acidosis.
High-concentration oxygen and oxygen-driven nebulisers can raise PaCO2 in hypercapnic patients — hence controlled oxygen to SpO2 88–92% and air-driven nebulisers.
Sputum or blood eosinophilia marks events that may respond better to systemic steroids.
Recovery takes 7–10 days on average; at 8 weeks up to 20% have not returned to baseline. Frequent exacerbations (2 or more a year) speed lung-function decline.

symptoms: Increased sputum volume and purulence (purulence suggests bacterial infection).
Reduced activity; may be confined to bed.
physicalSigns: Tachypnoea (over 24/min) and tachycardia (95/min or more) suggest respiratory failure (GOLD hospital classification).
Use of accessory muscles; pursed-lip breathing; wheeze or reduced air entry.
Central cyanosis; worsening peripheral oedema (cor pulmonale).
redFlags: Acute change in mental status, drowsiness or confusion
Hypoxaemia not corrected by Venturi mask or needing FiO2 above 40%
PaCO2 above 60 mmHg or pH 7.25 or less (life-threatening respiratory failure, GOLD)
pH below 7.35 or PaO2 below 7 kPa — treat in hospital (NICE)
Haemodynamic instability, or failure to respond to initial treatment
precipitants: Comorbidities: heart failure, PE, pneumonia may mimic or aggravate.

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Fever, focal signs, new consolidation on chest X-ray.
Orthopnoea, crackles, raised JVP, oedema; congestion on X-ray; echocardiography and natriuretic peptide.
Found in up to 5.9% of patients admitted with a suspected exacerbation; pleuritic pain, haemoptysis, no infective features — CT pulmonary angiography.
Sudden pain and breathlessness, unilateral reduced breath sounds; chest X-ray.

ruleIn.modalityTarget: All patients arriving at hospital; repeat frequently after starting oxygen and according to response
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Hypercapnia with acidaemia: pH below 7.35 = treat in hospital (NICE); pH 7.25 or less or PaCO2 above 60 mmHg = life-threatening (GOLD). PaO2 below 7 kPa = hospital.
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Hypercapnic acidosis persisting despite optimal medical therapy is the trigger for NIV. Compare with the patient's baseline PaCO2 and bicarbonate (chronic retainers have raised HCO3-).
ruleIn.normalValue: pH 7.35–7.45; PaCO2 4.7–6.0 kPa (35–45 mmHg); PaO2 above 10.6 kPa (80 mmHg) on air; HCO3- 22–26 mmol/L
pros: Gives PaCO2 and pH, which pulse oximetry cannot.
cons: Painful; VBG is accurate for pH and bicarbonate but not PaCO2 or PaO2 (GOLD).

clinicalManagement.title: Assess severity and setting
actions: Check RR, HR, SpO2, mental status and accessory-muscle use; take ABG with FiO2 recorded.

Treat in hospital if: severe breathlessness, poor or deteriorating condition, cyanosis, worsening oedema, impaired consciousness or confusion, on long-term oxygen, SaO2 below 90%, pH below 7.35, PaO2 below 7 kPa, new X-ray changes, significant comorbidity, rapid onset or not coping at home (NICE Table 7).
Grade hospitalised patients: no respiratory failure; non-life-threatening; or life-threatening respiratory failure (GOLD).

clinicalManagement.title: Controlled oxygen
actions: Venturi mask preferred (more accurate than nasal prongs); titrate to SpO2 88–92%.
Repeat blood gas after starting or changing oxygen to detect rising PaCO2 or falling pH.
High-flow nasal oxygen: ERS advises trialling NIV first in hypercapnic respiratory failure (cited in GOLD).

clinicalManagement.title: Short-acting bronchodilators
actions: Short-acting beta2-agonist (salbutamol) with or without short-acting anticholinergic (ipratropium).
MDI with spacer: 1–2 puffs every hour for 2–3 doses, then every 2–4 h by response (GOLD). Avoid continuous nebulisation.
If nebulised and hypercapnic or acidotic: drive with compressed AIR, give oxygen by nasal cannula at the same time; always prescribe the driving gas (NICE 1.3.11–1.3.12).
Continue or start long-acting bronchodilators as soon as possible before discharge.

clinicalManagement.title: Systemic corticosteroid
actions: Prednisolone 30 mg orally once daily for 5 days (NICE) — GOLD recommends 40 mg prednisone-equivalent for 5 days. Oral is as effective as IV.
Do not exceed 5–7 days (STS: 5–7 days preferred over longer courses).

clinicalManagement.title: Antibiotics when indicated
actions: Give if all three cardinal symptoms (more dyspnoea, sputum volume and purulence), OR two including purulence, OR needs NIV or invasive ventilation (GOLD).
Empirical choice by local resistance: amoxicillin–clavulanate, macrolide, doxycycline (tetracycline), second-generation cephalosporin, or a respiratory quinolone in selected patients (GOLD, STS).
Duration 5 days (GOLD; STS 5–7 days). Prefer oral when able to swallow.

clinicalManagement.title: Ventilatory support
actions: NIV is first-line for hypercapnic respiratory failure persisting despite optimal medical therapy (NICE 1.3.30; GOLD; STS — ward, HDU or ICU).
Deliver NIV in a dedicated area with trained staff; document a plan for deterioration and the ceiling of treatment before starting.
Stop NIV directly (no weaning needed) once the patient tolerates at least 4 h of unassisted breathing (GOLD).
Invasive ventilation: NIV failure, or contraindication to NIV; decide on functional status, BMI, oxygen need when stable, comorbidities and previous ICU — not age or FEV1 alone (NICE 1.3.34).
Respiratory stimulants (doxapram) only if NIV is unavailable or inappropriate (NICE); GOLD does not recommend them.
Confusion, FiO2 above 40% needed, PaCO2 above 60 mmHg or pH 7.25 or less: senior and ICU review now.

clinicalManagement.title: Adjuncts
actions: VTE prophylaxis for admitted patients (GOLD).
Fluid balance, diuretics if heart failure, treat comorbidities, nutrition.
Intravenous theophylline/aminophylline: GOLD does not recommend (side effects); NICE allows only as an adjunct if response to nebulised bronchodilators is inadequate, with level monitoring.
Smoking cessation support.

learningObjectives: Recognise, investigate and manage acute exacerbation of copd in the emergency department.

keyPoints: Controlled oxygen to SpO2 88–92% and repeat the blood gas.
Antibiotics for purulent sputum or ventilated patients, 5 days.
NIV for persisting hypercapnic acidosis, with a ceiling-of-care plan.
pitfalls: High-flow oxygen without a blood gas in a CO2 retainer.
Missing PE, pneumonia or heart failure as the cause.
Discharging without inhaler check, follow-up and rehabilitation referral.

patientEducation: Recognise exacerbation symptoms early; written action plan.
Complete the 5-day steroid course and know how to stop it.
lifestyleAndDiet: Not applicable in the acute phase.
mdtReferrals: Respiratory team; ICU or HDU for NIV failure or life-threatening respiratory failure.
dischargeCriteria: Clinically stable; comorbidities managed; laboratory and metabolic abnormalities corrected (STS).
Satisfactory oximetry or ABG if there was respiratory failure; spirometry measured; back on optimal maintenance inhalers with technique checked (NICE 1.3.41–1.3.45).
Long-term oxygen and home NIV needs assessed; patient and family confident to manage (NICE, STS).
nonClinicalManagement.followUpPlan: Review within 2–4 weeks (STS); pulmonary rehabilitation referral; consider home NIV if still hypercapnic about 2 weeks after the exacerbation (STS); exacerbation prevention per GOLD Chapter 3.

diagnosticCriteria.threshold: Increased dyspnoea and/or cough and sputum worsening over less than 14 days

RR above 24; accessory muscles; normal mental status; hypoxaemia corrected with Venturi above 35%; PaCO2 raised from baseline or 50–60 mmHg
RR above 24; accessory muscles; acute mental-status change; hypoxaemia not corrected or FiO2 above 40% needed; PaCO2 above 60 mmHg or pH 7.25 or less
3 cardinal symptoms, or 2 including purulence, or needs ventilation

adjustments: IV methylprednisolone if unable to swallow; STS range prednisone 30–60 mg daily or methylprednisolone 60–125 mg 2–4 times daily
